utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting. If I could remind you, sir, of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence that still applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, when we stopped yesterday, you were -- you had described Qerqiz's role in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move on and ask you some questions about Celiku's role in Lapusnik during the second half of May, June and July of 1998. During that time period, could you tell us approximately how many times approximately did you see Celiku in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you be more specific than that? More -- was it more than three times, more than five time, more than ten times? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe about ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any particular occasions that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember I have seen him twice, during the oath ceremony. Once when he brought a rifle to us, anti-aircraft 12.7 millimetre gun. Another time, I don't know why he came, but I have met him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when he brought the anti-aircraft weapon or gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We needed weapons and we had asked for them and I think it was in July when that weapon was brought to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where -- where did you see him bring the weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in oda in a room, near the headquarters. It was a large room where the clinic was situated, but I remember he brought it outside that room in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did anything happen when he brought it or did you just happen to be there when he brought it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just went to see how it looked like. We were very happy that we managed to have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did that weapon go? Did it -- where in Lapusnik did it end up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That weapon, we used it for some time. We took measures to transport it and then we took it to position number three. And it remained there until the war was over in July, when we withdrew from Lapusnik. It remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever see Qerqiz and Celiku together in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to describe how they interacted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the oath, or during other oath ceremonies, the Qerqiz was the one who gave the command. They were close by. At other times they talked between each other. Sometimes they talked in the presence of other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Qerqiz got orders from Celiku?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what we believed. All of us thought so, right from the beginning when it was said that the orders would be given to Qerqiz and Qerqiz would convey them to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from what you've just described or what you have just referred to, that meeting at the beginning with Qerqiz and Celiku, what else caused to you believe that Qerqiz got orders from Celiku, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was common knowledge to all of us. We all knew who our commander was and to whom he should turn for other orders or for other actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to give any specific examples of orders that went from Celiku to Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For example, I can tell you what I remember now, for the moment. It was once, when I wanted to address Celiku for something and then I went to Qerqiz first. I had my own reasons to meet him, but Qerqiz told me, You have to write an application in writing and to and that over to him. This is what I did. I handed over to him that application, and then he referred it to Celiku. But I didn't get an answer for that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any other specific examples of orders that you learned about coming from Celiku to Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all knew that our commander was Qerqiz and that above him, in Klecka, the person responsible for that territory was Celiku. And certainly there must have been someone or some others above him, but I don't know who they were. This was how the line was, up to Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if -- I asked you about orders, now I'm going to ask you about something else. Do you know in Qerqiz reported to Celiku about what was happening in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, regularly. They were in contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because when things happened in Lapusnik, he had to report, to take advice as to what to do further, what had happened and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question is: How do you know that he did that? How do you know that he reported and took advice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he went to regularly there to talk. For the moment, I can cite you an instances. It was on the evening of the 25th of July. We had been fighting all day long, and that was the first attack we had. When all sorts of weapons were used: grenades, rockets, poisonous substances. We were very tired. We couldn't resist any longer. This is what we thought, the Serb forces had come very close to us. In the evening, we met Qerqiz and Ymer at the crossroads that links the two points, position 1 and position 2. There we stayed for about half an hour or so. They too were tired. Ymer was almost sleeping. All of them were lying down. And when I asked them if someone could come to our rescue -- because I told them we were unable to keep guard during the night. Everybody was sleeping, probably because of that poisonous substance used against us. Maybe it was a particular bullet, 8 millimetre bullet that spread the poison. Out of that bullet a white powder or smoke came, and because of that, all of us who were in the positions started to have water running out of our mouths and all of us were exhausted. So that was a problem and I asked for reinforcements. After these conversation [as interpreted], they -- Qerqiz and Ymer went to Klecka for further consultations, to ask for advice and for help at the headquarters in Klecka, to bring new reinforcements because the order given to us was to stand up against the enemy and not to withdraw from the position. They went there that night. I don't know when they returned, but in the morning, they brought a cannon with them. Recoilless cannon. And it was in the morning that Ymer got killed and Qerqiz was close by. I didn't see it when he was killed. But this is what we heard and this is what we all believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After Ymer and Qerqiz returned from Klecka on the 26th, did you talk to either one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Ymer got killed on the 26th in position number five. I didn't see Qerqiz that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if he returned from Klecka on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean on the 25th? In the night of the 25th, they returned and brought with them that cannon that I mentioned. This is what I knew because until that day we didn't have a cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said you didn't see Qerqiz. How do you know he returned with the cannon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, we saw the cannon there. And they went to the headquarters to ask for assistance and then they had brought that cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But my question is: How do you know "they" brought the cannon? Let me take you back one step. When you say "they brought the cannon," who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I refer to Ymer and Qerqiz. Early that morning, when we went to the positions, I heard from someone that now we have a cannon. And a cannon has been brought to us. I didn't see them in the process of bringing it there, but I know that they went to ask for armaments and for reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there an occasion during this time period, May, June, and July, where you went to collect weapons from Lladroc? I may be mispronouncing that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Ladrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was in July, at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did that happen? Can you describe for the Court what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was near evening, I was close to the kitchen. Some soldiers approached me and told me that we have an order to go to Lladroc village and ask -- to collect weapons from people who had those weapons with legal authorisation. Hunting guns, pistols and so on. This is what we had been doing in villages close by when people were in legal possession of weapons. So we went to that village and collected the weapons which continued until late at night and we brought those weapons to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who gave the order to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. When we said we had orders to go, one of the persons who said that was in charge of position number four. And that -- I believed him when he said that he had taken that order, probably from Qerqiz. I can't tell you who -- who gave the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after you brought the weapons back to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We brought the weapons that night to Lapusnik. I gave one of the pistols to a soldier. And that same night I went to my village. I needed to go there to convince my mother to leave the house, because she was refusing to flee each despite the danger threatening my family. She refused to come over to the zone controlled by the KLA. When I returned in the evening -- in the afternoon, I met with some comrades had who been participating in that action. They showed me that because of that action of ours in Lladroc, Celiku had summonsed them to Klecka and had disarmed them. He had taken away their weapons for committing that action. And they told me that I also had to go there and hand over my weapon because we were punished for 15 days not to carry a weapon. That was usually the custom. I met Qerqiz at that time. He told me to go to Klecke together with my weapon. I don't remember whether he told me that I had to surrender the weapon and that I was condemned. But I went to Klecke. The disarming for a soldier for me in the war was something unacceptable. It was like telling him to go over to the Serb forces and do what he wanted. So I refused that order, I know that I have objected that order. I told -- I said that I'm not going to hand over the weapon because Celiku has not purchased that weapon for me. They are mine, and I didn't want to surrender them. They informed him about that. On the same day or on the next day other soldiers were taken away their weapons [as interpreted], and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few questions about what you have told us. Do you know why the -- the other soldiers and you were being disarmed? What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we had acted without Celik's knowledge. This is what we understood that to be. That action of ours was not authorised by Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And which action was not authorised by Klecka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I explained, the fact that we went to the village of Lladroc to collect weapons from the people there. And after that day, I heard that Celiku returned those weapons back to the owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went to Klecka who did you tell that you were objecting to the order or refusing the order? Who did you say that to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't go to Klecke. I talked with Qerqizi in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was a misunderstanding then. You did not go to Klecka after you were informed that you would have -- that you were being disarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to Klecka. I said that in Lapusnik I met the comrades who were with me when I -- the night before. They told me what had happened. And after a while Qerqiz came there and told me that I too had to go to Klecka. But I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you ever disarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened to the other soldiers who had been disarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons were turned to them, either that night or the next day [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I'm going show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's from P006. And it's on page 25. It's ERN U0072200. For the record, I have blocked out the name -- the writing underneath the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise what's in that -- depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It resembles the asphalt road, Pristina-Peja. Not the beginning of the road -- - but after the 20th of May it looked like that. It was -- that was built to prevent the enemy tanks. We did the same in position number two. We did the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after the 20th of May, in June and July, did it continue to look this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a while, this part of the road was blocked with gravel. Some 20, 30 cubic metres of sand or gravel. So I don't remember where that was. Often it happened that when the road was not blocked cars came from Peja, and we didn't tell -- we couldn't see them beforehand, so when they came up to that position, often they fired and that's why they blocked the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That photograph can be taken away. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, after the barricade was constructed on the road what would happen when people or cars came to the barricade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no great movements. The movements were very sporadic. It very rarely happened that cars or people came by, but when they did come, we asked them where they were coming from, where they were going to, the purpose for that movement and so on. The guard that was there asked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And could the guard who was there do this on his own or did he have to consult with somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the case of some civilian he didn't need to report it. When there was some soldier with a permission, he didn't -- he didn't need to ask someone. He just let them go. But if it was some foreign or strange person whom nobody knew, they stopped them. They asked for advice higher and then either they released the person or they didn't -- prevented him. Sent him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how would they ask for advice from higher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they were our own soldiers someone came to Qerqiz and asked him opinion, asked him what to do. But our soldiers on this side of the asphalt road didn't have great powers compared to those on the other side of the road, like the Pellumbi and the Guri units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Agim Bytyqi or Bujupi in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is from Arlat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did something happen to him during the period of time that we've been talking about, May, June or July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he came. But it must be June, when he came to Lapusnik from Germany. He was in his 30s, a young man from Arlat village. He had left his wife and one or two children in Germany and he had come to join the war. He stayed for approximately 20 days in Lapusnik. In the meantime in Lapusnik there was a small shop, or I would say a makeshift shop that sold drinks and beer as well. We would sometimes drink in front of this makeshift shop. During this time, the order came that the soldiers were not allowed to consume any alcohol at all, including beers. A day or two afterwards Agim was seen having a beer and his explanation was that the doctor advised him to drink a beer or two per day because he had problems with his kidneys. He was warned for not respecting the order and this action was reported in Klecka and soon after he was disarmed. Some of us insisted for his weapon to be returned to him, but they didn't return the weapon to him and I didn't see him afterwards. I don't know whether he returned to Germany or whether he went somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who reported the action to Klecka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Qerqiz. Qerqiz was a person who had seen him drinking a beer, who warned him and who reported this to Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know this because I was there when the order was issued not to consume alcohol. And as I said, he stayed there for a week and we talked together, and as I said, many of us insisted that the weapon was returned to him. We even pleaded to Qerqiz to intervene so that his weapon was given back to him, but this was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In July --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Actually we have to go into private session for this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to put back in front of you what what's been marked now as Prosecution Exhibit 169, the diary, with the assistance -- well, somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Perfect timing. If this could be given to the witness. Thank you. And if the usher could assist the witness to find page U0037004 to 7009 and on the English it's on page 12.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number for the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, on those pages are three entries that are marked July of 1998. Do you know when those entries were put into that book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that these entries were put in the end of August or beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were they put in there at that time based on your memory or based on notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had notes. I had an old notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so our record is clear here, when you say August or September, what year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to the first entry, for the first July 1998 entry which should appear on page 7004. It starts with: "The morning was calm with a few movements by the Serb forces." Can you just look quickly at that entry or -- take the time that you need, but are you able to tell us what that entry is describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This entry describes a day in the beginning and then this describes the movement of Serb forces in the direction of Fustica position. There was one of our units that was positioned there. It mentions some names and the event, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when in July this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It occurred in the afternoon of 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was there a battle in Fustica on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. And it lasted till late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you present -- did you participate in that battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did participate not directly in the battle, but we went there as reinforcement. We could not reach the positions but we stationed in the peripheral part of the village. There were others who had gone there as reinforcement. It seemed as if our soldiers had withdrawn from the position and the Serbs had seized with their attack. They were withdrawing as well. They had suffered many casualties. Probably they collected the bodies of their fallen members and withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now in the -- it beginning there's a some sentences which talk about Zenel. And it says: "He was Zenel's deputy," referring to somebody else who I won't mention, and it says "who had family ties with 'Qerqiz' and F. Limaj. As for his military training, he could not even handle a weapon. At my post in Lapusnik alone, his weapon went off accidentally three times! I told him not to come there..." Did that in fact happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But I believed that they had family ties. You could tell that they were close. It is true that I told him not to come to the position again. On the three occasions that he came to the position, his weapon went off accidentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is Zenel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And he then was the person in charge of the position in Fustica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, later in this passage it says that "a Serb officer threw his weapon, lifted his hands, came in the trench and was caught alive by our men." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then towards the end of the entry it says: "We interrogated the Serb officer. He later admitted that hes with an officer. He asked us not to kill him and said he could take us straight to the officer's tent and they could hand us over 50 tanks, cannons, machine-guns and a large amount of ammunition. He said they were going to withdraw in six days because about 600 members of an elite unit [Realtime transcript read in error: "Croatian"] consisting of mercenaries and Serbs were to arrive in order to take over Lapusnik and open the road to Peja. Our command, headed by F. Limaj, was not interested in this and later that night, sometime after midnight, they poured two litres of petrol on him in Blinaje and closed the block on it." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that during the translation now I heard that 600 elite member Croats. It's not true, it is 600 metres -- members of special units. Mercenaries. Not Croatians but Serbs, who were about to come and attack the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was a Serb officer in fact captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you present when he was captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. And according to what is written here, one can understand that "we" might include myself. But this we refers to the members of the Kosova Liberation Army, not myself personally. I was not there when he was taken. I know that that battle took part [as interpreted]. There were some of my people who took part there. The Serbs thought that there were not -- no KLA members in that part and they thought that area was mined. They went there in order to demine it. They opened a fire when the Serbs approached at 20 or 30 metres and Serb soldiers were killed, many of them were killed on the spot from our soldiers. One was wounded. The Serb officer through his weapon away and he surrendered. He entered the KLA position and surrendered. He then was interrogated that night. And he pleaded to be released and to be allowed to go to Quka e Komoranit where the Serbs were positioned. And he told us that there was ammunition and there were tanks. The number here is 50; it could be that there were 50 tanks. And he said a possibility for to us enter the officer tent and to take those weapons and ammunition. At that time, it was very difficult to go to the Albanian border for weapons because the border was mined and people were getting killed at the border with Albania. This Serb was taken somewhere, to Shale or I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was just going to interrupt you to say -- to ask you to please get back to the story about the Serb officer and then you just did. So what happened to the Serb officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was taken, he was questioned when we went to assist in Fustica we were with Ymer, with Qerqizi and with five other persons in the vehicle. There were others from Kroimire who came there. There was Luan, and Shukri Buja and it must be them that -- who took this officer because Shukri Buja didn't stay there for long. I later heard that this officer, military officer, was burned. Maybe he was not an officer realistically, but this is what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question was: How did you know all of these things that happened to this Serb officer? How did you know that he had surrendered, been interrogated and was later killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went to assist we already met with the soldiers of Fustica position. In conversation with them, we found out how this event developed. In the beginning I said that I had two of my own soldiers there, and when I discussed with them as well, they told me the same story.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At any point did you yourself see the Serb officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When we arrived he was already removed from there. One of our injured soldiers was also removed from that place, and they were taken to Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever see the body of the Serb officer after he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it in Blinaje. I don't know whether the person was a KLA members or a civilian. He was maintaining KLA vehicles, and on the road to Blinaje, on the side of the road, there was a burnt body. The boots were not burnt, and this person who I mentioned above, told me that this was a body of the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know the identity of this Serb officer, his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you told us before that a rule about drinking beer had been communicated to you while you were at Lapusnik. Were there other rules that were communicated to you at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did have rules, yes. The rules that were communicated to us were to be disciplined. There were rules about guard duty, about lining up, about salute, regulations about the kitchen and for the food. It wasn't an army without rules. It was an army, actually, with military rules and it was an army that was even more disciplined that the Serb army that maybe had a greater tradition than us. We obeyed and abided to these rules because we were all volunteers and we all wanted to have rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, how were these rules communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them when we were lined up, given to us orally, and in some cases even on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who would communicate the rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Qerqizi. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would anybody else communicate the rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, with the assistance of the usher, I'm going to ask that Prosecution Exhibit 156 be placed before you. Witness can you -- can you take a moment to look at that? I showed this when you were preparing for your testimony, did I not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yeah, this is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see this book while you were at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see these, but there were -- there was talk about the rules. But I didn't see it. I know the oath. I am familiar with the oath ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is the oath -- is that the oath that -- that you took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just look through the other rules in the book and tell us if you are familiar with any of those rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. Unfortunately between the Defence bar we only have one copy of this rule book. So I wonder if Mr. Whiting, which he is perfectly entitled to do, is going to go into a textual analysis of it or part of it, I wonder if we might have a few moments to have this copied. I don't know if that would be a convenient moment, or a slightly earlier moment than usual for a break. That's not actually my application, it's just to give us some time to get this photocopied. I'm sorry. We just haven't had it done before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there only one copy available, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand from Mr. Younis that we had provided multiple copies, but I can understand that they have been misplaced. I have only my own copy. I don't know if -- Mr. Younis an always prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Younis. I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're being volunteered again, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. Why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Getting to learn the signs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have previously received a copy of this from Mr. Younis. I am appreciative of receiving another copy of this. I was not going to raise an issue with having or not having a copy at this time. However, I am grateful to Mr Younis and the Office of the Prosecutor for giving me a copy at this time, as I'm sure is Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that we can carry on, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, if we can go back to my question. Are there any rules that you remember being communicated to you during your time in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said also earlier that there were rules, rules on lining up on the salute. With the exception of the fact that that changed after a little while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did the salute change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially we saluted with our closed fist. Very soon after, maybe after 20 days, the order came no longer to salute with the closed fist but with an open hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the oath change to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't change.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you keep looking through and I know it's long text and just -- are there any examples of orders that you have given us -- you have described the orders generally, but are there any examples that you see in this book that you remember being communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For example, on page 10.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we don't have the rules. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To leave and demand respect of rules, preservation of military secret and so on. We all abided by those rules. We didn't allow anybody to approach our positions. I have read those rules some days ago, but they are written in very small letters and there are many, but I have -- I may say that this is how we respected these rules. And the oath was the same. So most of them we followed, like, for example, the maintenance of weapons. Travel authorisation. The rules on the health conditions. Personal hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These were all rules that were communicated to you while you were in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That can be taken from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you have testified that there were two oath ceremonies at Lapusnik. Can you tell us to the best of your recollection when those oath ceremonies occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One occurred at the end of May. It was at the end of May. There was a small number of soldiers, and the other one occurred because the number of soldiers grew in June, and therefore it was necessary to hold another ceremony. But all of us participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were these ceremonies held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Lapusnik, in a courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember where the courtyard -- which courtyard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a courtyard near the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is -- is that near the kitchen where you identified yesterday that you and the other soldiers would eat, would have your meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe those oath ceremonies for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said that by the end of May for the first one. It may have been that both of them occurred in June, one early June, the other after mid-June. I'm not certain about the timing. But it was a very short distance between the two, in terms of time. With respect to your question, I kindly ask you to repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will. My question was: Could you describe the oath ceremonies. What happened at the oath ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were lined up, all of us, we raised the flag and after the flag was raised, the command was given to stand. Then the content of the oath was read out, and that was it. It was a short -- a brief ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you recall who ran the ceremony or was in charge of the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second ceremony -- for the second ceremony, even in the first, I think, Celiku was present along with some others both in the first and in the second ceremony. Kumanova was with him, Musa Jashari, Nexhi, Qerqizi. These were the people that I remember. There may have been other members who came from Klecke, soldiers or otherwise, certainly, but I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You referred to Musa Jashari. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a relative of the Jashari family which was massacred in Prekaz. And at that time Musa was -- played the role of the liaison among the headquarters. At least this is what I knew him to stand for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Liaison among which headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Its headquarters in Klecke, in Likovc, other headquarters that were in the region. Like a liaison officer, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you made a reference --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding political issues I think mostly. He was dealing with the political aspect. At least this is I think. I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you made a reference to Nexhi. Who was that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nexhi was from Terpeze. Usually was Celiku's driver. When Celiku came to Lapusnik, Nexhi was the one on the wheel of his Jeep or car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you have given a number of names of people who were at the ceremony. Do you remember who was in charge of the ceremony or ran the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who ran the ceremony, I'm not sure whether it was Qerqizi or someone else, but I remember that Celiku read the text of the oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now a clip. This is from Prosecution Exhibit P35.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could have the Sanction, please. And there an a little moment at the beginning which is not relevant. But then we'll get to the part that I'm going to ask you questions about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I will be vigilant, courageous and disciplined, ready at any time without sparing my own life, to fight to defend the sacred interest of the homeland. This is it how Fatmir Limaj explained the decisions of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's all, yeah. We can have the lights back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you see the -- the oath ceremony on that clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that resemble in any way the oath ceremony that you have described that occurred at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was exactly like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the oath ceremony that is in the clip, were you present for that oath ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was held somewhere else in the vicinity of Klecke and Luznica, in July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because it was conveyed also in the media. It was broadcast in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And aside from Celiku, did you recognise anybody else in that clip that we just saw? Just pertaining to the oath ceremony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very dark on my screen, but I could tell Celiku, Kumanova, Musa Jashari, Nexhi. But I could tell them more or less because of the uniform and the shape of his body, of Nexhi's body, because it was rather dark for me to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we break, there is now before us the written submissions for which we have been anxiously waiting. I notice in them that it is suggested that we should not rule on that until we have dealt with the outstanding motion to receive the evidence of a previous witness. There are to be written submissions in that. Can they be ready from the Defence on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see there are volunteers for certain tasks. Very well. They will be expected by Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are considering applying for leave to file a very brief reply to the Defence' response and we had already planned to submit that on Monday. And brief will be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Monday is the last day for written offerings of any type in this matter, then. We will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may briefly make clear for record that although I had originally been tasked with drafting the response to the Prosecution motion, it wasn't actually me who drafted the final response. In relation to the response to the Shukri Buja motion, it's unlikely that it will be me who will be drafting that response either. So it's perhaps a little premature of me to make the concession that it will be possible to draft a response by Monday. I spoken to those who probably are going to be doing in and they can probably do it by Monday, but if the Chamber were minded to grant until Wednesday, I am told that would be much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would in the Chamber's view be inconvenient and an unnecessary length of time given the issues. I am afraid that we must stick to our position, Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So if you can convey that to those who are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I want to go back to Lapusnik in May, June and July of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1998. I want to remind you also that you have water and if you want to have some water, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, during May, June and July of 1998, was there a prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a house that was called a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you first hear about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. It could be end of May. But I'm sure that in the beginning of June the prison was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn where the prison was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was near the kitchen. It was a house on the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the house in a compound or was it standing separately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The neighbourhood there was called Lagjja e Voyvodve and there was a house there. There was a group of houses, several houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit P005.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And we could switch to the Sanction, please. And I'm going to ask Mr. Younis to go in right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, for the record, I'm showing you what's marked in P006 as building A1. Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the main building in this yard. There are other buildings, one or two other buildings, and this is what I referred to as the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask -- I'm going to ask Mr. Younis to go -- take a look around the yard. If you could stop there, please, and go back. And for the record, we're looking at the wall in the compound, and I don't believe there is a picture from P006 of this. No. But so I'll just describe it. It's a wall with a white building on the other side of the wall. Witness, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Younis has assisted me. It's marked as number 3 on U003-2456, which is page 1 of P006. Pretty soon I'm just going to let Mr. Younis do this. Can you tell us what this building is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Behind this wall in this building, several soldiers were stationed and several from the territorial defence, that is to say, civilians who were guarding the village. We cannot see the yard here, but I believe that the yard is a little bit steep and that's where we held the oath ceremony. It's not the yard here that we see, but the yard behind the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'll ask Mr. Younis to continue going around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now we're back to looking at building A1. Witness, did you ever see people being detained in this being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Mr. Younis to go to A4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This image is looking at the door of building A4. It's page 7 of P006. Do you recognise this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if Mr. Younis can go into building A4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise it from the time of war because both this one and the building shown before this were used as prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember anything in particular about this room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that on the right side, the concrete wall, you can see that it's a little bit wider from inside. Maybe it's not seen clearly from here but you can see it's wider. Now you can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And are you -- are you referring to the right side of the image that you're looking at right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for the record, the image is page 10 of P006. And if we could now go into building A5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this door and window? This is looking at A5. It's page 11 of P006.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes it's the same as it was this 1998, I mean the door, but the building itself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how was this room used in 1998 in June -- May June and July -- or let's say June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one and the other one were used as prison. There were occasions when even in the other building there were people. It was kind of a pre-detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which was a pre-detention unit? The one we're looking at right now or a different building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said that this one was used as prison and the one that we saw earlier. But the other building at the entrance, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at A1 again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this building. This house was used as a pre-detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you referring to the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The house in front with a terrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the reasons could reflect that the witness is referring to A1. And, Mr. Younis if we could go out to the road outside of this compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, we're now looking at the main gate from the outside of compound A. Do you recognise that gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It had the same colour. Even the smaller entrance, here on the right, was exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that smaller entrance on the right, do you recall where that leads? Or do you know where that leads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door on the right, when you open it immediately after a metre there's a staircase that leads you up. And then on the right side there is another entrance leading to two rooms, one after another. The first room is a bigger one. I don't know the size of the second room. I think it's smaller. If you continue straight there are stairs that take you to the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now, if we could go to the compound across the road. And for the record, we're in compound B. We're now looking at building B1. It's on page 18 of P006.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered this building many times. After the 29th of May, after that battle, this house was used as a staff for several days. There was a TV in this house which we used in order to watch the news. We used it for gatherings or for guests during holidays. There's another door below it. There is a kind of a cellar which is known seen on this picture. It looks the same except for the roof. It seems that it is a new roof. The house itself is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask Mr. Younis to pan left and stop there, please. We're now looking at page 19 of P006, building B2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness there are two buildings here. B2 is in the forefront and behind it is another building which is yellow brick. Witness, do you recognise either of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise all of the buildings in this yard. And they haven't changed, with the exception of the fact that on the right side which is not -- cannot be seen here, there was another building which was covered, but was kind of open without a wall and could have served as a garage or as a storage place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these buildings that on the image - again, it's page 19 of P006 - can you tell us what these two buildings were used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where the kitchen was. In the basement of the big building the kitchen was there. That's where the stoves were. And the building on the right, maybe it was used for a day or two but I don't know for what. It was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you refer to the buildings, please by their colour. One is a white building and one is a yellow building. In which building were the stoves? The yellow building or the white building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tall building, the one with the yellow colour, in the corner you can see some doors. That's where the basement is and that is where the kitchen was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the kitchen that you referred to earlier where the soldiers would come for that are meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the building. And that's what it was used for til the end of July, when we withdrew from Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We can take that off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want it ask you some questions about the prison on the other side of the road. During May, June and July of 1998, did you yourself go to the prison, go into that prison compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went alone and I went with Ymer, but not in May. In June and in July. This is when I went. I don't remember going there in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Approximately how many times in June and July did you go into that compound where there was a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that I was there six, seven or eight times. I went there several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could anybody go to -- into that compound, that prison compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't hear the first part of the question, the part when you say "a person".

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask it again. Could anybody go into that compound where the prison was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was guarded. And for the soldiers it wasn't allowed to go there. The persons who could go there were designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who were the persons who could go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning it was kept like a secret. I don't know if all of the soldiers knew about it. But shortly after, they all learned about it. As for the persons who could go in it was Ymer, Qerqiz, Timi, Zenel, mainly these persons. And the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who were the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shala and Murrizi were the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also were allowed to go in to the prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it was desirable, but I could go there with Ymer and I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why were you allowed to go into the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that in the beginning I went there with Ymer. But on two or three occasions I went alone. Once it was reported to me that one of the arrested persons knew my family, my brother; that's why I went. On one occasion I took a prisoner there and on another occasion I went to look for two persons there is. These are the occasions when I went there alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions that you have referred to as Shala. Do you know -- in -- in June and July of 1998, did you know Shala's real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was his real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Haradin Bala. I didn't know him from before. But there I learned whose son he was. I knew his father and I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who is his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know his father as Bala but as Selman Haradinaj. I knew which village he came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What village did he come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Korretice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you first meet Shala, Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think where the kitchen is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did you learn his real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Someone introduced him it must have been Ymer who introduced him and we spent some time together and we had a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did he stay in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was there till the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Till the end...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I didn't see him in the last days of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say you believe he was there until the end, are you referring until the end of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I said, until the end of July. Until we stayed in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From the beginning of June until the end of July what were the duties of Haradin Bala, Shala, in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Haradini did not have an another duty but to stay outside or inside the door, or the gate of the house that was called a prison. I saw him on the day when a friend had brought 12 black uniforms. I went to that house to collect a uniform for myself and that's when I saw him. I don't know of any other tasks that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see him inside or outside the gate of the house that was called a prison? Did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him inside, in the first building, the entrance that I described. I saw him outside and I saw him in the kitchen yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say "in the first building," which building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the building which is close to the gate, to the brown-coloured gate. Or attached to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The gate of the prison compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you describe how Haradin Bala looked -- how he looked physically in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He looked well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I mean how tall was he, his age, things like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was over 40 years old. Could be about 180 metres [as interpreted] tall. That's what I think. He had a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about his teeth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. His teeth were a little bit damaged due to an illness and they were very split.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember what colour they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not white. I said they were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you saw Haradin Bala in the compound where the kitchen was, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually he stayed there. He was kind of a guard. He didn't have a specific task. On one or several occasions, I saw him carrying food from the kitchen and bringing the food inside. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Bringing the food inside where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was your relationship with -- like with Haradin Bala during June and July, 1998? What kind of a relationship did you have with him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had good relationships with everyone, and especially with Haradin. We were in good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe what kind of a soldier he was or what kind of a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a nice soldier. He was very calm and well behaved. I have never seen him annoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there another man at Lapusnik who used the pseudonym Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know who -- who this person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was a young man from Shale village. I think that he had an injury on his right leg, and due to this injury, he was crippled, unable to walk straight. He was a good soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During June and July of 1998, did you know the real name of this soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ruzhdi Karpuzi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What were his duties at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see Ruzhdi in May. I saw him in June, in the beginning of June in the room which I described as the one which had a TV and where we watched the news. Ruzhdi would sit in the corner and would take notes, keep records. This was his duty in the beginning but not the duty until the end. By the end of June he then went to position number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know how long he stayed in position number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Until the 24th, on the evening of the 24th of July. On the 24th of July, I went to look for him and to call him to come to position number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did he do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did that. I asked, I don't know who I consulted, whether it was Ymer or Qerqiz. I went there and I took him with me to position number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that in the -- in the beginning of June he was in the room that had the TV and where you watched the news. Was that room in the -- in the compound where you would go to eat? Is that the room that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what kinds of notes and records he was keeping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was keeping notes that were necessary for Lapusnik. On one occasion, I saw him writing or rewriting a statement of a prisoner from one paper to a more neat paper. This is what he told me. I didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what other -- any other kinds of records that he kept? You said that -- notes that were necessary for Lapusnik. Do you know any -- can you give any other examples of notes or records that he kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that house, in the lower part of that building, there was a cellar where they kept cigarettes and other material. It was kind of a logistic place. I think that he also kept records about the logistics and other necessary notes about the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, going back to Haradin Bala, you testified that he "looked well" when I asked you about a physical description. What was his physical condition like during June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I described that. He looked in good condition. I don't think he gave me the -- any indication of not being well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from Haradin Bala and Ruzhdi Karpuzi, do you know of any other soldier in Lapusnik to used the name "Shala" during June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Haradin Bala and Ruzhdi Karpuzi look alike?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well I'm going to object to that as being leading. He can ask him how -- well, he knows how to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think in the circumstances it's a -- a rough but acceptable method of asking for a differentiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did Haradin Bala and Ruzhdi Karpuzi look alike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I said that Ruzhdi Karpuzi was lame in one length.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you ever said that they look alike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I have mentioned that in the first interview, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First interview with whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you say they looked alike in that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew his condition at home and his physical condition. And in my opinion then and now, I don't think that Haradin Bala is guilty. I knew that a person was released who was arrested then, and I think that I didn't need to say what I knew about him, thinking that he too might be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see Haradin Bala after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You referred to his physical condition. What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant that I heard that he was suffering from a heart disease. There was someone else, a person called Luftari in Lapusnik who died because of heart -- a heart disease. That was the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you said you didn't -- it was your opinion then and your opinion now that Haradin Bala is not guilty. Why -- why is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I have never heard and never seen him maltreating anyone in Lapusnik before that time or after that time. And given the way that I know him, I don't believe he is a person that can maltreat anyone else. That's my belief. It was then and it's still now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You referred to another guard by the name of Murrizi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In June and July of 1998, did you know Murrizi's real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He knew my name. But I only knew his name -- his first name, not last name. Or to put it better way, I knew where he was from and where he lived. I had seen him before the war several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. If you could tell us what you knew about him, in terms of his name and where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that he came from Klecka. I knew that he lived in a village very close to Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you say you knew his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think so. If I didn't know it then, I must have learned it later. But I think I knew it since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you know it to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew it to be Agim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn at some point his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His last name I learned late. People who live in that neighbourhood, irrespective of their written last name in official documents, they referred to one another and Klecka and I thought his last name would be Klecka, that is Agim Klecka. But later I found out that in the official papers his last name is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you find it out to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 17th of June, 2003, 17th of June, 2003, were you shown photographs of individuals on different pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know in which of the interviews they were shown, but they were shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you able to select people from the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'm going to somehow you some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could switch to the Sanction and the first one is U0034037.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, was this page of -- was this page of photographs shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you circle number 3 in right Agim Zogaj, Murrizi, at number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it seems like my handwriting. I have marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you identify that photograph as Murrizi, Agim Zogaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Next I'm going to show you U0034038.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This too is marked by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you recollect photograph 8 as Haradin Bala, Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that your writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next one is U0034039. Is -- is that your handwriting in red on -- on this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you read what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "This person resembles Qerqiz."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this how Qerqiz looked during May, June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He had the same face, but he had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to U0034040. Is that your writing under number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you recognise that photograph as Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that these be given a number and that they be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What precisely are "these"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These photo sheets --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The four photo sheets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- with the numbers that you have read in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received under seal as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The for these photographs will be P172, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, they have to be under seal because they have the witness's signature on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, can you recall the first time that you went into the compound that was used as a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was early June, and there were rumours about a big spy. This is how they described him. And I was close by. I met Ymer and he told me, Come with me to meet someone. And this is how I went there for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have often thought about it because these two buildings are very similar to each other. But I am certain that in one of them I went. I think it was the lower building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I'm showing you again an image for P005.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for the record, it's an image showing the doors of both A4 and A5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you need your glasses? Do you recall which -- was it one of those two rooms you went into the first time? When you went into the prison for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm very certain about one of the two rooms. But as I said, they are very similar inside, so I am not sure which is which.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went into the compound, you were with Ymer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember there was anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see anybody -- any soldiers or guards in the compound on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think there were, but I can't tell you who they were. Maybe someone came with us, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you see when you went to one of those two rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the door was open, there were three or four persons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did they look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With exception of one all seemed well. He was lying down. He tried to stand up, but he couldn't. Ymer told him, Stay where you are. And I think he was either sick or he was not in a good condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were any of the three or four persons restrained in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went there again - I can't say it was the first or the second time - I think someone was tied. I'm very certain that someone there was tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you observe anything else about the room or the three or four persons when you went on this first occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Only that the person as I said couldn't stand up. I was focussed on him more, and I remember that -- I remember his clothes more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever learn who this big spy was that you had heard about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
